newsitem.title: USA: Perry says U.S. two-war strategy faces reality.
newsitem.headline: Perry says U.S. two-war strategy faces reality.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry said on Thursday the United States cannot give up its two-war strategy as critics proposed because the possibility of having to fight two Gulf-like wars at nearly the same time was simply a fact.

"You cannot wish away the reality that you might be faced with two major regional conflicts (wars) as long as you are trying to maintain your presence as a global superpower," Perry told reporters at a year-end press session.

Perry said he was confident U.S. forces could fight the two wars because the Defence Department was ready to send a war force into South Korea in 1994 during the confrontation over North Korean nuclear facilities, and still keep a force in reserve if there was a second war in the Middle East.

"The analysis we did at that time, of the force structure required to deal with that, has been reasonably well verified," he said. "Nothing has happened in the last four years that has called that into question.

The two-war strategy has been criticised by members of the U.S. Congress who say the post-Cold War U.S. military is not big enough to carry it out and there have been reports that some of the Defence Department's generals agree.

Army Chief of Staff Gen. Dennis Reimer is not one of them. He told reporters on Wednesday almost the same as Perry said, that the possibility of the United States having to fight two wars at nearly the same time was simply a fact of life.

But Perry said the question of how to shape U.S. forces to continue to be ready to fight two wars despite low defence budgets was the major question to be answered by a sweeping Quadrennial Defence Review the Pentagon is conducting.
He said the crucial question was whether the U.S. military should continue to assume the second war would not start for about six weeks or revise that assumption and reshape U.S. forces.

He said the military found when it planned the separate Korea and Middle East war forces in 1994 that assuming the second war would start in one or two weeks would have stressed present U.S. forces, particularly the planes that would have to rush additional U.S. forces into the two wars.

Perry said as he has before that he does not believe the United States will ever have to fight two wars at the same time, so long as potential enemies know that one war would not leave too few U.S. forces in reserve to fight a second one.
